name: simgrid
desc: Studies behavior of large-scale distributed systems
why: A discrete-event simulator for studying large distributed systems, a real research tool you can run at home to model networks and clusters.

brief.what_it_is: SimGrid is a framework for building simulators of distributed computer systems. You write a program against its API (in C, C++, Python, or Java, per the homepage) that describes a platform such as clusters, networks, or data centers, plus the applications running on it. The simulator then predicts performance, including time and energy, and can also be used to debug and profile real MPI applications. It is a library, not a graphical tool or a command-line simulator that runs user scripts. The brew package also ships companion executables (graphicator, simgrid-mc, smpicc, smpicxx, smpirun, tesh, and others), but I did not see their usage in the pages I fetched.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says SimGrid exists to "prototype, evaluate and compare relevant platform configurations, system designs, and algorithmic approaches" for distributed applications. The docs add that it has been developed for about 20 years by a research community, initially in France and the U.S.A.
brief.how_it_works: Simulation models for platforms such as commodity clusters, WANs and LANs, DSL peers, and data centers are provided ready to use, and the APIs let you build a simulator on top of them. The docs describe the models as fast, scalable, and experimentally validated. The docs also mention a prototypical model checker for formally checking simple algorithms and applications.
brief.install_notes: The homepage lists Linux, Mac OS X, and Windows as supported platforms. The docs say Windows is supported only through WSL. The brew formula installs the executables listed in the input. I did not see any install, build, or first-run steps in the pages I fetched, so the exact procedure for writing a first simulator is unverified.
brief.standout: Compared with a typical CLI simulator, SimGrid is an embeddable library with its own models and APIs. Its executables are secondary tools, and the scout note's pitch of running it at home to model networks and clusters understates that you write C, C++, Python, or Java programs against it.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning active. The homepage advertises current version SimGrid 4.1 and the documentation site is live, but I did not see a release date or last-commit date in the pages I fetched.
brief.caveats: Not a point-and-run tool: you must write a program against the API, and the pages I fetched contain no example commands. Windows support is only via WSL. The model checker is described as prototypical. The license is LGPL-2.1-only per the docs. The brew caveats field is empty. The scout note calls it a tool you can run at home, which overstates how turnkey it is.
quotes: Technically speaking, SimGrid is a library. It is neither a graphical interface nor a command-line simulator running user scripts.
SimGrid is free software (LGPL license) available on Linux / Mac OS X / Windows, and allows users to write simulators in C++, C, Python, or Java.
Most of the time, SimGrid is used to predict the performance (time and energy) of a given IT infrastructure, and it includes a prototypical model checker to formally assess these systems.

judge.reason: A research-grade simulator lets you model distributed platforms and applications to explore performance, energy use, and even model checking—an unusual window into systems behavior.

entry.title: SimGrid
entry.tldr: A research library for simulating distributed systems, so you can predict how clusters, networks and data centers behave without building them.
entry.deeper_look:
SimGrid is a framework for building simulators of distributed computer systems. You write a program in C++, C, Python, or Java that describes a platform (clusters, LANs, WANs, DSL peers, data centers) and the applications running on it. The simulator then predicts performance, including time and energy. It can also be used to debug and profile real MPI applications.

The homepage says it exists to "prototype, evaluate and compare relevant platform configurations, system designs, and algorithmic approaches" for distributed applications. A research community, initially in France and the U.S.A., has developed it for about 20 years. Ready-made models for common platform types are described as fast, scalable, and experimentally validated, so you build on them instead of writing your own network model.

The idea underneath is that you can study a system too big, too costly, or too awkward to run for real by simulating it. You change a topology or an algorithm and compare results, repeatably, on one laptop. SimGrid also includes what the docs call a prototypical model checker, for formally checking simple algorithms and applications.

The docs are blunt: "Technically speaking, SimGrid is a library. It is neither a graphical interface nor a command-line simulator running user scripts." The brew package also installs companion tools such as smpicc, smpicxx, smpirun, tesh, and simgrid-mc. The pages the brief covers did not show how they are used.
entry.install:
brew install simgrid
# Needs a C++ toolchain, and you write your own program against the API in C, C++, Python, or Java. On Windows, support is via WSL only.

entry.whats_unique: It is an embeddable simulation library with its own validated platform models, not a ready-made simulator. It can also run real MPI applications on a simulated platform.
entry.caveats: Not a point-and-run tool: you must write a program against the API, the model checker is described as prototypical, and the brief found no example commands.
